title: SRE: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives & Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
document_body:
Summary:

This page consolidates Redwood Inference SRE standards for SLO definitions and measurement, error budget policy and escalation, capacity planning cadence and forecasts, reliability initiatives and prioritization, incident review (postmortem) standards, the operational tooling stack, and canonical runbooks for on-call responders. The goal is a single, actionable reference SREs and service owners can use to ensure consistent reliability practice across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

1) SLOs & Error Budgets

Overview:
- SLOs express user-facing reliability and performance targets. We partition SLOs by product surface (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private control plane) and by user-facing metric (availability, request latency, embeddings throughput).
- Error budgets are calculated on a rolling monthly window (30-day sliding window) unless otherwise noted for critical control-plane services where we use 7-day rolling for faster feedback.

Primary SLOs (examples):
- Hosted API availability (ingress+model execution): 99.95% monthly uptime (error budget = 0.05% downtime per 30d).
- API request latency (inference request): p95 <= 200ms for lightweight models; p95 <= 800ms for large multi-GPU models (these are model-classified SLOs; see model catalog).
- Embeddings throughput (batch endpoints): 99% of requests served under configured batch timeout (T_batch) for Dedicated pools.
- Private control plane (customer-managed): control-plane API availability 99.9% monthly.

Measurement and tooling:
- Primary metrics source: OpenTelemetry metrics ingested into Prometheus/Thanos with Grafana dashboards.
- Synthetic checks: global HTTP synthetic probes from 5 regions (us-east1, us-west1, eu-west1, ap-southeast1, ap-northeast1) run every 30s; synth failures feed SLO and alerting.
- Error budget computation: daily job that computes rolling-window SLO compliance and publishes to the SRE dashboard and to the "SLO status" channel in Slack.

Error budget policy and burn actions:
- Green (<= 25% of budget burned in 30d): normal operations; can proceed with planned releases.
- Yellow (25% < burn <= 50%): engineering leads notified; reduce non-critical risk (defer low-impact changes), increase monitoring cadence.
- Orange (50% < burn <= 80%): release freeze for non-critical features; schedule immediate reliability review; consider temporary traffic shaping or routing to lower-cost model variants to reduce latency-induced failures.
- Red (> 80%): emergency mitigation required; engage on-call extended team and product leadership; consider capacity increase, temporary throttling, and customer notifications per escalation playbook.

Burn rate thresholds (examples):
- If burn rate > 4x over a 6-hour window -> page SRE on-call (PagerDuty).
- If remaining error budget < 10% with forecasted trend -> automatic stage gate on canary rollouts.

2) Capacity planning

Cadence and ownership:
- Quarterly capacity planning cycle (90-day horizon) owned by SRE + Infra + Product. Monthly refresh for near-term forecasts and burst preparation before major launches.
- Owners: SRE capacity lead (primary), infra-finance (cost modeling), product (demand forecast).

Forecasting process (high level):
1. Collect signals: historical traffic (API requests/day), token-per-request distribution, model mix (which models are in production), seasonality factors from marketing/product, committed Dedicated reservations, and large-customer pipeline events.
2. Run baseline forecast: 90d median, p75, p95 scenarios. Include growth factor from sales pipeline and upcoming product launches.
3. Convert to GPU-hours and instance types using model performance profiles (see quantization-profiles).
4. Add safety buffer: 20% for p75, 35% for p95 by default; adjust by service criticality.
5. Publish recommended capacity plan and cost delta; get approvals from Infra and Finance for reserved purchases.

Autoscaling and burst policy:
- Always prefer autoscaling within Dedicated pools before manual provisioning. Configure autoscaling windows to match observed request burst durations (default cooldown 120s).
- Burst capacity providers: short-term burst pool and cross-region failover. Reserve small hot pools for ultra-low-latency customer tiers.

Capacity runbook checklist (pre-launch):
- Verify canary model performance under synthetic load (p95 latency, GPU memory, KV cache hit rates).
- Run end-to-end load tests at p95 forecast x 1.2 for 1-hour sustained window.
- Confirm autoscaler policy and scaling playbooks are exercised in staging.
- Confirm alerting thresholds and dashboards are published to on-call rotation.

3) Reliability initiatives and prioritization

Initiative intake:
- Reliability initiatives are captured as RFCs with measurable objectives and KPIs (reduction in p95 latency, error budget savings, cost per token). Use the Reliability Initiative template.
- Prioritization is driven by impact (error budget risk reduction), effort, and business cadence. SRE leadership reviews candidate initiatives bi-weekly.

Examples of initiatives:
- Prefix caching improvements to reduce average token cost by 12% for chat workloads.
- Kernel selection tuning for Llama-like architectures to lower p95 by 20ms.
- End-to-end tracing improvements to reduce incident MTTD by 30%.

Success metrics (must be defined in each RFC):
- Baseline metric, target metric, measurement method, rollout plan, and rollback criteria. Initiative must pass a post-rollout evaluation at 30d to be considered successful.

4) Incident review standards (postmortem)

Classification and severity:
- Sev1: Customer-impacting outage or sustained P99 customer-visible degradation > 30 minutes or major data-loss risk.
- Sev2: Partial outage or degradation affecting subset of customers or functionality > 60 minutes.
- Sev3: Minor impact, degraded telemetry, internal-only issues.

Timeline for postmortem publication:
- Initial incident timeline and communication within 24 hours.
- Full postmortem including timeline, root cause analysis, contributing factors, and action items within 4 business days.

Postmortem requirements (blameless):
- High-level summary for executives and customers.
- Timeline of events with exact timestamps and decision points.
- Root cause analysis with evidence (logs, traces, metrics).
- Contributing factors across people/process/tech.
- Action items with owners, due dates, and verification steps.
- Follow-up review at 30d to verify completion and measure effectiveness.

Severity-based communication matrix:
- Sev1: Exec/Customer comms drafted by SRE + PM within 1 hour; public status page update every 30 minutes until stabilised.
- Sev2: Status page updates hourly; targeted customer comms based on affected segments.
- Sev3: Weekly summary in the on-call rotation notes.

5) Operational tooling (canonical stack)

Dashboards and metrics:
- Grafana + Prometheus/Thanos for metrics and long-term retention. Pre-built SLO dashboards per service and an SLO summary dashboard for org-level view.

Tracing and debug:
- OpenTelemetry + Jaeger for distributed traces. KV cache and model execution spans instrumented. Standard trace sampling: 10% for production, 100% for onboarding canaries and error traces.

Logging and error aggregation:
- Centralized logs in Elasticsearch/Opensearch with Kibana dashboards. Alerts anchored to aggregated error rates and tail-latency spikes.

Alerting and paging:
- PagerDuty for on-call paging. Alerts must include runbook link, required ownership, and a short checklist for first responder actions. Use standard alert severity mapping aligned with SLOs.

Automated runbooks and playbooks:
- Store runbooks as Confluence pages and link them from alerts. Keep playbooks concise: checklist-style with required commands and telemetry links.
- Alert -> Runbook -> Mitigation -> Escalation.

6) Runbooks (canonical examples)

All runbooks should follow this structure:
- Purpose and scope
- Impact and symptoms
- Preconditions and required access (roles, AWS/GCP projects, service accounts)
- Immediate actions (10-minute checklist)
- Diagnostic commands and queries (PromQL, CLI, curl examples)
- Mitigation steps (short-term)
- Recovery steps (long-term)
- Post-incident follow-up actions
- Owner and escalation path

Example runbook: "inference-api-high-latency"
- Purpose: Steps to diagnose and mitigate high tail latency on the inference HTTP API.
- Symptoms: p95 latency spike > 2x baseline; increased 5xx rate > 0.5%; alerts: grafana/inference/p95-latency-high, grafana/inference/5xx-rate-high.
- Immediate 10-minute checklist:
  1) Acknowledge alerts in PagerDuty and set incident channel.
  2) Check global synthetic probes and identify region(s) affected (Grafana Synthetics panel).
  3) Verify recent deploys in the last 60 minutes (CI/CD dashboard).
  4) If deploy identified -> rollback canary or pause rollout.
  5) Check GPU utilization and queue lengths on Serving runtime (kubectl top / gcloud compute ssh + nvidia-smi).
  6) If queues are growing and CPU/GPU not saturated -> investigate downstream rate limiting or KV cache miss storm.

- Diagnostic queries (examples):
  - PromQL: 100 - (sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m])) by (service) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) by (service) * 100) -> availability
  - PromQL tail latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service))
  - Check KV cache hit rate: sum(rate(kv_cache_hits[5m])) / sum(rate(kv_cache_requests[5m]))

- Short-term mitigations:
  - Scale inference workers by +25% if autoscaler not reacting (manual scale) and there is spare capacity in the region.
  - Temporarily route new traffic to a lower-latency model variant for affected customers.
  - Increase model batch timeout config if timeouts causing retry storms (config change with rollback plan).

- Recovery and verification:
  - Monitor p95 and error-rate for 30 minutes post-mitigation.
  - If stable, run a controlled canary replay of suspended traffic for 1 hour before full restore.

7) Governance and reviews

- SLO review: SRE + product review SLOs semi-annually and after any major product change (new model class, new hosting mode).
- Runbook review: on-call owners must review and confirm runbook accuracy quarterly. Changes must include a short changelog.
- Reliability initiative postmortem: every initiative must report measured impact at 30d and 90d; results folded into capacity and roadmap planning.
